summary:
Finland does not criminalise trans people, and the sources reviewed record no trans-specific violence against a visitor: no assault, mob attack or police-brutality case involving a trans traveller appears in the material. The hate-crime figures below are national aggregates, not an incident series involving visitors.

Police recorded 1,808 suspected hate-crime offences, the highest total ever logged, with defamation and the most common types being defamation and assault. The Police University College reports the sexual-orientation and gender-identity-or-expression category rising across six reported years, from 72 cases to 241. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2026 gives the same headline total of 1,808 suspected hate crimes, a 13% increase since 2023, and identifies sexual orientation and gender identity as recurrent motives, present in 12% of cases.

The Criminal Code contains no hate-crime offence. Motive is captured only in police reports, so sexual-orientation and gender-identity-motivated incidents are counted as reported suspicions rather than as charges. A visitor has no separate legal exposure: there is no sodomy-style offence, no public-order offence keyed to gender expression, and no law requiring a trans person to disclose status to police.

Legal gender recognition operates under the 2023 statute: applicants must be 18, down from a proposed 15 with guardian permission, observe a 30-day reflection period, and may change the registered marker only once per year. The former requirement to be sterilised or otherwise infertile and to hold a mental-disorder diagnosis applied until April 2023 and no longer binds. Finland was one of three countries in a six-country Investigate Europe investigation that wrote infertility requirements explicitly into law; the last such requirement in that group was phased out at the end of June 2025, and the people subjected to the earlier regime form a documented legacy cohort.

Conversion practices have moved into the courts and Parliament. Finland's first conversion-practices case was prosecuted as assault, with convictions in March, and Parliament endorsed a citizens' initiative to ban conversion practices by 125-49 in March, though a full statutory ban remained pending.

Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since 1 March 2017, and a 2018 amendment to the Maternity Act recognised both women in a same-sex partnership as mothers from the moment of birth rather than through later second-parent adoption. Discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, and on gender identity and expression since 2005, is prohibited under Section 8(1) of the Discrimination Act, whether the discrimination is based on fact or assumption; the Act on Equality between Women and Men also covers gender identity, and Parliament extended it in 2014 to employment, goods and services, education and health services.

Gender-affirming care for minors is delivered through the country's two centralised gender identity units. The Council for Choices in Health Care revised its clinical recommendations for gender dysphoria under age 25 in 2020, prioritising psychosocial therapy over medical transition; because these are recommendations rather than mandates, puberty blockers remain available case by case and cross-sex hormones can be considered where identity is of a permanent nature causing severe dysphoria. A Seta survey found over 40% of trans respondents entirely unable to access the care they needed, most reporting extended waiting times, which is the most concrete indicator of what a trans visitor needing unscheduled care should expect.
tangentialFactors:
Finland's government has itself judged that trans travellers face risk abroad rather than at home. In March 2025 Finland updated its travel advice for transgender citizens travelling to the United States after reports of border difficulties following the US 'two genders' executive order. That advice is outbound guidance issued to Finland's own travellers and is not an assessment of risk within Finland.

Violence figures that do exist are aggregate and dated: Finnish police reported 73 violent attacks and assaults against LGBT people in 2018, a 27% increase on 2017 and the only hate-motive category to rise that year. In November 2019 the Institute of Health and Welfare reported that LGBT children and youth face significantly more bullying and more physical, psychological and sexual violence than heterosexual peers, and are more likely to suffer violence at home. Neither figure isolates trans victims or visitors.

The country's trajectory compares with its neighbours in a specific way: Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden explicitly wrote infertility requirements into legal gender recognition law, and at least 11,000 people were subjected to such conditions across the six countries investigated, Sweden being first in 1972 and keeping the requirement in force for 40 years. Finland ended its requirement in April 2023.

Since December 2023 there is no extra deferral period on blood donation for men who have sex with men. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1971, homosexuality was declassified as an illness in 1981, discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation became a criminal offence in 1995, and 'transvestism' was removed from criminal law in 2011.
localsOnly:
Gender recognition applications under the 2023 law are made by Finnish residents: 18 years of age, a 30-day reflection period, and one marker change per year. The 2020 Council for Choices in Health Care recommendations on dysphoria under 25 shape what public gender clinics offer residents, but they are recommendations, so blockers and hormones remain available case by case.

Resident family law rests on the 1 March 2017 marriage equality date, when same-sex marriage and joint adoption took effect; registered partnerships had run from 2002 until the same day, conferring the rights of married couples except adoption and a joint surname, and including immigration rights for a foreign same-sex partner. Stepchild adoption became legal in 2009, and an April 2019 law passed 122-42 gave lesbian couples full maternity pay and parentage rights without intra-family adoption. Surrogacy remains illegal for all couples.

The 2017 marriage law entered Parliament through the 'Tahdon2013' citizens' initiative, which collected more than 162,000 certified signatures against a 50,000 threshold, far above the organisers' 250,000 target, and became the first initiative passed by Parliament, legalising same-sex marriage in December 2014 by 101-90. The Constitution allows any initiative carrying 50,000 valid signatures to be put to Parliament, the same mechanism now used for the conversion-practices ban.

Support organisations operate nationwide: Seta, founded 1974, Trasek for trans and intersex rights, and Rainbow Families. Gender-affirming care for minors runs through two centralised gender identity units. Gay and trans venues and Pride events operate openly, with an estimated 100,000 attending 2018 Helsinki Pride, and public visibility dates to a 2010 gay rights panel on state broadcaster Yle TV2 and the first public gay demonstration in 1981.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 1,808 suspected hate-crime total is attributed to different reporting years by different sources: the Police University College release of November 2025 describes the figure as recorded in 2024, while ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2026 presents the same number as the 2025 figure. Which calendar year the record total belongs to is unresolved in the sources reviewed.

Signature counts for the 'Tahdon2013' initiative are given as over 162,000 in one source and over 166,000 in another. The discrepancy is unresolved and does not affect the outcome.

Whether Parliament has since enacted a full statutory ban on conversion practices, as opposed to endorsing the initiative 125-49, is not resolved in the sources; the Annual Review states a full ban remained pending.

No source in the inventory documents a trans visitor to Finland being refused entry, questioned about trans status at the border, denied a marker correction on Finnish documents, or refused service. Absence of such a record here reflects the sources reviewed, not a verified negative finding.

Statistics on hate-motivated violence against trans people specifically, as distinct from the combined sexual-orientation and gender-identity category, are not available in this inventory.
